name: Cloud infrastructure (utility computing)
title: Why Loudcloud failed, and when cloud computing became viable
question: Why did Loudcloud's utility computing fail, and when did the cloud become viable?
answer: Loudcloud (1999) sold managed hosting as utility computing, went public in March 2001 and sold its hosting business to EDS in 2002, keeping the software (Opsware, bought by HP for $1.65B in 2007). Every customer still meant dedicated hardware. AWS (2006) sold the same promise on virtualised, shared servers, which Xen (2003) and VMware made cheap.
verdict_reason: Hardware virtualisation matured in 2003; AWS launched S3 and EC2 in 2006.

constraint.name: Hardware virtualisation
constraint.detail: Without slicing one server among many customers, 'utility' computing was outsourced dedicated hosting with a utility's price promise.

crossing.text: Xen hypervisor released (2003); VMware ESX in production use.

graveyard.name: Loudcloud
graveyard.how: Sold its managed-hosting business to EDS in 2002; renamed Opsware

evidence.text: Xen, the open-source hypervisor later used by EC2, was first released in 2003.
